channel.title: Virtual Machines :: FAU Cyber Security Club
channel.description: A virtual machine is your lab. All practice happens here — not on your host. Break it. Reset it. Repeat. That is the whole point. This section covers why VMs matter, how to get one running, and what tools to use.

item.title: Why Virtual Machines
item.description: A VM runs a full operating system inside your current one. It is isolated — what happens inside stays inside. You can break it completely and roll back to a snapshot in 30 seconds. That is the whole value proposition. Real-World Uses Security professionals use VMs constantly. Malware analysts run suspicious files inside VMs so the malware cannot touch the host. Penetration testers spin up target VMs to practice exploits before using them on a real engagement. Blue teamers deploy hardened VMs to test detection rules without touching production systems. Developers use VMs to replicate a customer’s environment exactly. The common thread: controlled isolation. You can experiment without consequences.

item.title: Setting Up a VM
item.description: Pick a hypervisor (see Tools), download an ISO, create the VM. That is the whole process. The details differ by tool, but the steps below are universal. Step 1 — Choose a Guest OS For security work, start with one of these: OS Why Kali Linux Comes with most security tools pre-installed Parrot OS Lighter than Kali, good for older hardware Ubuntu Clean slate, you install what you need Kali is the default choice for offensive security. Ubuntu is better if you want to learn Linux from scratch without preinstalled noise.

item.title: VM Tools
item.description: A hypervisor runs the VM on top of your host OS. There are several. Pick one that fits your hardware and OS. Options VirtualBox Free. Cross-platform (Windows, macOS, Linux). The most widely used option for beginners. Works on almost any hardware Solid snapshot support Slightly worse performance than VMware Download VMware Workstation Pro / Fusion VMware Workstation runs on Windows and Linux. VMware Fusion runs on macOS. Both are free for personal use now.
